rows.l1_text: When data analysts report to managers without a technical background, the most common mistake is to start right away by listing model parameters and statistical indicators, with the result that the audience grows more confused the more they listen, and the findings that really matter are instead drowned out.
What managers care about is not how ingenious the algorithm is, but whether the analysis results can support the next decision.
Therefore, a report should first present the conclusion, and then back it up with data layer by layer.
Second, it is worth learning to tell stories.

Rather than saying "the customer churn rate in a certain region rose by eight percentage points", it is better to describe how an old customer turned to a competitor because of delivery delays, and then bring out the causes behind the data.
Such narration gives abstract numbers warmth and also makes them easier to remember.
Finally, make good use of visualization.
A clear line chart is often better than ten pages of tables, but charts must be concise, highlight the key points, and avoid piling on decoration.
With a clear conclusion, a vivid story and intuitive charts, the three combined, a report truly has persuasive power.
In an increasingly competitive business environment, the speed and precision of corporate decision-making often determine success or failure.

The data dashboard is precisely a management tool born for this: it integrates the massive information scattered across systems such as sales, logistics and customer service, and presents it centrally on the same interface in the form of charts.
Managers do not need to leaf through lengthy reports one by one; they only need to browse this dashboard to grasp the whole picture of the business at a glance.

With the help of real-time monitoring, core indicators such as order volume, conversion rate and inventory turnover are continuously refreshed as the business progresses, enabling the team to promptly catch subtle fluctuations.

More crucial is the early-warning mechanism: once an indicator exceeds a preset threshold, the system automatically issues a prompt, reminding the responsible persons to investigate the cause and adjust strategy, thereby resolving potential risks in their infancy.
It can be seen that the data dashboard not only improves information transparency but also pushes companies to shift from "judging by experience" to "letting the data speak".
On an e-commerce platform, what color the “Buy Now” button should be often does not depend on the designer's intuition, but on A/B testing.

So-called A/B testing is randomly dividing the users who visit the website into two groups: one group continues to see the original orange button, called the control group; the other group sees the newly designed green button, called the experimental group.
The other conditions of the two groups are kept the same, so any difference can be attributed to the color itself.
After the experiment lasts several weeks, the team compares the conversion rates of the two groups, that is, the proportion of users who click the button and ultimately place an order.
However, a slight lead in the numbers is not enough to settle the matter, because chance fluctuation can equally cause a gap.
Analysts must also test the significance of the results, judging whether the difference goes beyond the range of random error.
Only when the preset standard is reached will the platform change the color across the board.
What takes the most careful thought in wedding preparations is often not the standard of the banquet, but deciding whom to include on the guest list and whom to leave off.

Once the number of tables for the wedding banquet is fixed, it is hard to increase or decrease it at will, so the couple usually have to weigh things repeatedly: which people must be invited, and which relationships, though close, have been out of contact for many years.

There is also a proper order in sending out invitations: for the closest relatives of the parents' generation, it is appropriate for the family elders to invite them in person at their homes, while colleagues and friends can have the invitations passed on through others, and propriety in etiquette is often valued more than the form itself.

As for gift money, on the surface everyone understands without saying, but in fact it contains a set of conventional standards: closeness or distance, and old accounts of mutual dealings are all quietly settled in this red envelope.

The role of the master of ceremonies lies in coordinating the whole event, both looking after the elders' dignity and leaving a relaxed atmosphere for the young people, so that the whole banquet strikes a balance between liveliness and solemnity.
A respectable wedding is, rather than a contest of show, more a careful handling of social obligations and human relations.
In Chinese business banquets, drinking-table culture is often regarded as a subtle language of communication.
A seemingly ordinary dinner is in fact an implicit negotiation in which both sides probe each other's sincerity and weigh cooperation.

Baijiu, because of its high alcohol content and strong aftereffects, has long occupied the center of banquet occasions; when the host says "bottoms up", the drink in the glass must be drained in one gulp, otherwise it may be interpreted as contempt for the host.

Urging others to drink is not simply an act of drinking, but a set of conventional rituals in social entertaining: juniors toast elders, subordinates toast clients, and the rim of one's glass should be slightly lower than the rim of the other person's glass, to show respect.
However, this logic of measuring sincerity by capacity for alcohol is being questioned by more and more young professionals.
Some tactfully decline on grounds of health, and others substitute tea for alcohol, trying to find a balance between social obligations and their own personal boundaries.
When "being able to drink" is no longer equated with "being able to get things done", this drinking-table culture that has lasted for many years is also quietly loosening.
At half past six in the early morning, the food market is already bustling with voices.
In recent years prices have kept climbing, a bunch of greens has gone from two yuan to five, and pork in particular makes people shrink back.
For retired elderly people on a fixed income, this means that every cent has to be spent where it counts.

Their shopping can be called a field of study: first they walk around the market once, silently memorizing the prices quoted at each stall, then turn back to choose carefully; some even convert the unit prices of three stalls into how much per jin, striving to see them clearly at a glance.

When bargaining, they are not in a hurry to speak, but first praise the vegetables for being fresh, then take the opportunity to ask whether it could be a bit cheaper, with a tone neither servile nor overbearing, and a sense of proportion handled just right.
Most stall owners know perfectly well, and when they meet such old regular customers, they often smile and waive the odd change.
Behind the careful budgeting is not stinginess, but a generation's almost instinctive reverence for the two words "thrift".

Before the stalls close in the evening, the discounted vegetables are the most popular, and several old people gather in one spot to swap tips; that composure and tacit understanding is the earthy warmth of everyday life that cannot be found in a supermarket's refrigerated shelves.
In recent years, community group buying has risen rapidly, quietly reshaping the way urban families do their daily shopping.

Its core is not some technological breakthrough, but a trust mechanism with neighborly relationships as its bond: group leaders are mostly full-time mothers or retired residents of the compound, who, relying on their long-accumulated network of acquaintances, post product information and tally orders in the group chat, and have next-day-delivery goods delivered in bulk to the pickup point downstairs from their own homes.

For consumers, this model eases the double anxiety of price and convenience at the same time: the platform uses pre-sale to reduce inventory risk and thereby gives up part of its profit; and cutting out the cost of last-mile delivery makes the price of fresh produce clearly lower than at traditional supermarkets.
More worth noting is its social effect: modern neighbors who were originally distant from one another have, through the small talk of each pickup, re-established a minimal level of contact.

Of course, a group leader's authority depends heavily on personal reputation, and once quality control slips, the community's stickiness and repurchase rate will quickly collapse, which is perhaps exactly the hidden worry that makes this model hard to scale up.
Fast fashion relies on constantly updated trends and low-price promotions, filling a wardrobe with new items in a short time, and it also easily leads people into a cycle of consumerism.
Many clothes are worn only a few times before being set aside because the style is outdated, the fabric is thin, or the quality is poor.
By contrast, “buy less but buy better” emphasizes choosing clothing that is durable, well-fitting, and easy to match.
It does not pursue quantity, but values quality, craftsmanship, and long-term usage value.
People who practice decluttering will tidy their wardrobes more carefully, keeping only the things they truly need and often wear.
This approach can both reduce waste and make one's personal style clearer and more stable.
Although the initial cost may be higher, buying classic styles is usually more economical and also better fits the idea of sustainable living.
In recent years, "escaping Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou" has gradually changed from a joke into a real life choice.
More and more young people, after struggling for several years in first-tier cities, decide to return to their hometowns and start over in that familiar small city.

What drives them to make this decision is often not a lack of ability, but a sober weighing of options: soaring housing prices and long commutes let the cost of living keep devouring their income; while the hometown has a relaxed pace and warm human feeling, and that long-missed sense of belonging is something no salary can replace.
Of course, returning home does not mean retreating.

Some bring the experience accumulated in big cities back to their local area, open studios, and take part in their hometown's industrial transformation; there are also those who were full of expectations at first but in the end left again because of limited opportunities.
It can be seen that there is no better or worse between returning home and staying, and the key lies in how each person defines the kind of "worthwhile life" in their own heart.
Interpersonal relationships in the workplace often drain more energy than the work tasks themselves.

Many newcomers naively think that as long as they do their own part flawlessly and keep a polite distance from colleagues, they can stand safely in the organization; yet the reality is that when disagreements arise within a department, or even invisible factions form, the pressure of "picking a side" will quietly close in on everyone.
Choosing to get close to a certain leader may indeed bring resources and protection, but it also means the risk of taking the blame for them at critical moments.

Facing a superior who is especially strict in their demands, rather than guessing their thoughts and catering to their preferences, it is better to build a way of getting along based on professionalism and trust: report progress proactively, admit mistakes frankly, and carefully assess the limits of what you can bear before making a promise.
Real professional security is never obtained by attaching oneself to someone, but comes from irreplaceable ability and clear personal boundaries.
Ride-hailing has brought great convenience to people's travel, yet the safety hazards lurking behind it cannot be ignored.

In recent years, reports about drivers deliberately taking detours, verbally harassing and even assaulting passengers have been common, and such incidents often occur late at night, on remote road sections, or when the driving route is clearly abnormal, while passengers and drivers are strangers to each other, so once danger is encountered, it is often hard to judge the other party's true intentions, and also hard to seek help in time.
Faced with these risks, passengers should take preventive measures on their own initiative.

Before getting in, be sure to check whether the license plate number and driver information match what the app shows; during the ride, you can use the platform's trip-sharing function to send your real-time location and estimated arrival time to family or friends, so that others can keep track of your whereabouts at any time.
At the same time, you should try to choose the seat in the back row on the right, keep a suitable distance from the driver, and avoid revealing too much personal information.

If you encounter improper charges, deliberate detours or other inappropriate behavior, passengers must not swallow their anger, but should keep evidence such as recordings and screenshots, promptly file a complaint with the platform, and call the police when the situation is serious.
Only when the platform, the regulators and the passengers all make joint efforts can the line of defense for travel safety truly be built up.
When we browse goods, search for keywords, or linger a few extra seconds on a certain piece of clothing, the platform's backend has already quietly begun recording.
After being integrated by algorithms, these scattered behavioral data gradually piece together a "user profile" of us.

The profile contains information such as age, region, income level and hobbies, and the platform then, on this basis, attaches different labels to each person, such as "student crowd", "mother-and-baby group" and "price-sensitive type".

Subsequently, enterprises segment the huge population according to consumption habits, put similar users into the same category, and push different advertisements and offers to each, and this is what is called precision marketing.
For merchants, doing this can lower promotion costs and raise the closing rate; for consumers, it both brings convenience and conceals the risks of privacy leakage and the "information cocoon".
Therefore, understanding how one is being labeled and learning to manage authorization of personal information has become an essential quality in the digital age.
Qingming is a traditional festival on which the Chinese express their grief and remembrance.

On this day, people help the old and lead the young to cemeteries outside the city to sweep the graves, removing weeds, wiping the tombstones, and setting out flowers and offerings, in order to honour their ancestors and express remembrance of those who came before.
This ritual looks simple, yet it carries memories of blood ties; it lets young children learn for the first time where they come from.
However, with the advance of urbanisation and the awakening of environmental awareness, traditional ways of tomb-sweeping are quietly changing.

Quite a few families choose online tomb-sweeping: in a virtual memorial space, they offer a bouquet of electronic chrysanthemums and write a few words from the heart, so that relatives scattered in different places can gather at the same moment.
Some worry that this form is too frivolous and dilutes the solemn atmosphere; others believe that as long as the intention is sincere, the medium does not matter.
However the form evolves, the emotion that Qingming carries remains the same: it reminds modern people in their busyness not to forget to look back at those who shaped us.
In recent years, our country's views on marriage have been undergoing a quiet change.

In the past, divorce was often regarded as something embarrassing to mention; now, more and more people admit that, for a relationship that cannot be repaired, it is better to end it frankly than to maintain it reluctantly.

It is against such a background that the divorce cooling-off period came into being; it is not meant to stop people from ending their marriages, but to leave a little room for a buffer for impulsive decisions.

According to the regulations, if both parties divorce by agreement, they must first submit an application, after which either party may withdraw it within thirty days; when the period expires, they must also appear together before they can receive the divorce certificate.
This cooling-off time often lets couples re-examine their differences: some are reconciled because of it, and others confirm their choice more clearly.
However, the cooling-off period also brings new difficulties.

For a party who is suffering domestic violence, waiting another thirty days means one more degree of risk; and when it comes to child custody and the division of property, if the two sides never manage to reach agreement, they can only turn to litigation.
How to strike a balance between safeguarding the stability of marriage and respecting individual freedom remains a topic of continued discussion in society.
In the residential compounds of many cities, friction between property management companies and residents' committees has a long history.

The former, entrusted by the owners, are responsible for security, cleaning and facility maintenance, and charge property fees accordingly; the latter, as grassroots mass organizations of self-government, mostly undertake functions such as policy publicity and dispute mediation.

The boundary between their responsibilities is vague to begin with, and once problems such as chaotic parking or the occupation of public space arise in a compound, the two sides easily shift blame onto each other, accusing the other of overstepping or being absent.

A prominent conflict in recent years has centred on the control of maintenance funds and public revenue: some owners doubt that the property company's accounts are clear, and so jointly form an owners' committee, hoping to restrain its behavior through collective negotiation and defending their rights by law; the residents' committee, for its part, tends to mediate in the middle, to avoid intensified confrontation affecting community stability.
This tension is not entirely negative; to a certain extent it forces service quality to improve, and also prompts all parties to gradually explore the path of consultative co-governance.
When the smog keeps getting worse and the meteorological department has issued a warning, residents should put health protection first.

The elderly, children and people with sensitive airways should reduce unnecessary outdoor activities; when going out, it is best to wear a mask that meets the standard and to avoid busy traffic hours and road sections.
After returning indoors, one should promptly close the doors and windows and turn on the air purifier to keep lowering the PM2.5 concentration.
When choosing an air purifier, one should not focus only on appearance, but should comprehensively consider the clean air delivery rate, filter life, applicable area and noise level.
If it is for the living room, one can choose a model with a more ample airflow; if it is placed in the bedroom, one should pay even more attention to quietness.
In addition, only by replacing the filter regularly and ventilating moderately when the air quality improves can protection and comfort reach a better balance.
In the field of data analysis, Python has almost become a "standard" for practitioners, and pandas is the most favored library among its tools.

As for the reasons, first, pandas provides the intuitive structure of the data frame, which is like a programmable spreadsheet with rows and columns clearly distinct, and an analyst needs only a few lines of code to complete tedious operations such as filtering, grouping, merging and handling missing values.
Second, Python's syntax is concise and close to natural language, so even people who did not major in computer science can pick it up fairly quickly.

More importantly, analysts can write repeated cleaning and statistical steps into scripts to automate the process: whenever new data arrives, they only need to run the script to get results within a few minutes, which both avoids oversights in manual operation and makes the analysis process reproducible and verifiable.
In addition, an active open-source community keeps contributing new extensions, letting the capabilities of this set of tools keep growing.
In recent years, "996" has gradually evolved from the internal rules of individual companies into an industry convention that is accepted by default.

With work starting at nine every morning, ending at nine every night, and running six days a week, long overtime is packaged as the virtue of "striving", and has even become an implicit standard for measuring whether employees are loyal.

In such an environment, colleagues cannot help comparing with one another who leaves later, and so the phenomenon of "involution" appears: ever more time is invested, yet the final returns have hardly increased.

Faced with this kind of drain, some young people choose to "lie flat", protecting their lives by lowering their desires and refusing to compete; others take the Labor Law as a weapon, and demand through arbitration and litigation that companies pay overtime wages.

The law clearly stipulates upper limits on daily and monthly overtime, but in actual enforcement, factors such as the difficulty of gathering evidence and the fear of unemployment make many people hesitate.
Real change perhaps lies not in individual endurance or escape, but in bringing the rules back to the negotiating table.
In banking business, the core link of loan approval is risk control, that is, identifying and guarding against potential losses.
In the past, loan officers mainly relied on interviews and paper materials to judge whether a borrower was reliable, which inevitably carried a subjective color.

Nowadays, banks use big data to build credit scoring systems: the system aggregates the borrower's income, repayment record and debt ratio, and then converts them through a statistical model into a score; the higher the score, the greater the likelihood of repaying on schedule.
Banks accordingly predict the default rate, and decide whether to lend, as well as the amount and the interest rate.

At the same time, anti-fraud systems monitor abnormal behavior in real time, for example the same device repeatedly applying for loans in a short time, and once suspicious signs are found, they automatically raise an alert and hand the case over for manual review.
However, models rely on historical data, and when the economic environment changes drastically, predictions may become inaccurate, so they must be continuously calibrated.
The young couple have worked in the city for many years, and recently began seriously considering living with their parents, or at least living nearby.

With their parents growing older, living together would make daily care more convenient and could also ease the pressure of housework and child-rearing; but they worry that the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law relationship would become complicated, and also fear that differing living habits would cause friction.

The wife is used to getting up early and quietly preparing breakfast, while the mother likes to chat while watching television; the husband hopes to rest alone on weekends and does not want to be always arranged into family activities.
After repeated discussion, they realised that independence does not mean distance, but that a balance must be found between family affection and boundaries.
In the end, they rented two apartments in the same residential compound, so that they can look after each other when needed and also keep their own rhythms of life.
As parents gradually grow old, the question of supporting them is placed before every child: send the elderly to a nursing home, or keep them at home and care for them personally?
In many people's view, filial piety means being together day and night, and handing one's parents over to strange caregivers seems to be a way of shirking responsibility.
However, the pressure of reality does not allow everyone to do this.
Children have to work and raise their own children, and often can hardly spare even one full day of company.
Professional nursing homes, on the other hand, are equipped with medical staff and round-the-clock care, and for elderly people who are disabled or have chronic illnesses, are actually safer.
The real dilemma lies not in which residence to choose, but in how to balance responsibility and emotion.

Some people hire a caregiver to come to the house in the daytime and go home themselves in the evening to talk with their parents; others send their parents to a nursing home but insist on visiting every week.
Caring for the elderly has never been an either-or multiple-choice question; what matters is letting the elderly still feel loved and respected while they are being cared for.

With the spread of social platforms, netizens leave massive numbers of comments every day, and behind these seemingly scattered words there often lies the public's true attitude toward products, events and even policies.
Text analysis is precisely the technical means of extracting useful information from this kind of unstructured data, and sentiment analysis is one of its most widely applied branches.

Its basic process is roughly as follows: first clean the comments, removing advertisements and duplicate content; then, with the help of word segmentation technology, cut continuous sentences into independent words, because in Chinese there are no natural spaces between words; then extract keywords and, by checking against a sentiment lexicon or a trained model, judge whether each comment leans positive, negative or neutral.
Companies and government departments can monitor the trend of public opinion on this basis and promptly discover potential crises.
However, the complexity of language poses considerable challenges to analysis: irony, internet slang and contextual differences often cause machines to misjudge the author's true intent.
When a group meal breaks up, the bill is often more likely than the food to make people feel awkward.

Some people are used to rushing to treat everyone, seeing paying the bill as a way of expressing friendship; others advocate splitting the bill equally, believing that everyone paying for themselves is cleaner and more comfortable.
The former fear losing face, and the latter fear owing a favor; these two states of mind silently pull against each other at the cashier's counter.

Nowadays WeChat Pay has given this difficulty a compromise: one person pays first, then starts a group payment request in the chat group, the system automatically calculates each person's share, and participants only need to tap to confirm, and the money quietly arrives.
The whole process requires no talking about money and no repeated polite refusals, which both preserves the dignity of the host and spares the guests any psychological burden.

Of course, technology can only resolve awkwardness in form, and the real sense of propriety still depends on the relationship between the people involved: with a close friend of many years, it is not worth worrying about who pays a little more; with someone you have just met, clear accounts are instead a form of respect.
At family gatherings, young people often use internet slang and buzzwords, leaving the elders confused and baffled.
For example, the younger generation says "broke my defenses", "absolutely amazing" and "got it handled", and the elders do not understand, nor do they know why these words suddenly became popular.
Young people find these expressions light and fun, able to convey emotions quickly; the elders, however, worry that language is becoming chaotic and affecting communication.
In fact, many internet expressions originate from memes, short videos and trending events created by netizens, and they carry an obvious group-culture flavor.
Because of different growing-up environments, a generation gap has appeared between the elders and young people.
Faced with this difference, family members can patiently explain the meaning of each meme, and can also discuss together which expressions are suitable for formal occasions.
As long as both sides are willing to listen, internet slang can also become a bridge connecting different age groups.

In the third week of my mother's hospital stay, I have almost figured out the routine of that ward: in the early morning the nurse comes to take her temperature, in the afternoon the sunlight crawls aslant up onto the bedside cabinet, and the evening is the hardest time of the day to get through.

Caring for a patient is not merely keeping watch; it is more like a long test of endurance: the folding bed is too narrow, the coughing at night is too frequent, and during the day I also have to deal with work and bills.

Relatives and friends who visit bring fruit and comforting words, saying things like "you'll be out of the hospital soon"; I accept them with a smile, but in my heart I know very well that recovery is never a straight line.
The nurse taught me how to turn her over and how to record her intake and output, and in those trivial movements lies a kind of almost clumsy tenderness.
Gradually I understand that what is called caring is really handing over a part of your own time, in exchange for a little peaceful breathing for the other person.
As the plastic restriction order is gradually rolled out in many cities, people have begun to re-examine the plastic-related details of daily consumption.

In the past, many consumers were used to casually asking for disposable plastic bags when buying goods at the supermarket, and were also used to using plastic cups and plastic straws for takeout and at drink shops.
These seemingly convenient choices, however, turn into hard-to-degrade garbage within a short time.
In recent years, more and more people have chosen to carry reusable shopping bags and reusable water bottles with them, turning reducing plastic use into a way of life.

Reusable shopping bags can not only be washed repeatedly and used for a long time, but can also carry heavier items; reusable water bottles let people hydrate at any time while commuting, attending class and traveling, avoiding frequent purchases of bottled drinks.

Although changing habits takes time and reminders, once this choice gradually blends into homes, campuses and workplaces, it is no longer merely an individual act, but becomes an important force promoting the sustainable development of cities.
In recent years, Hanfu, as a kind of traditional clothing carrying deep historical memory, is returning to the daily lives of urban young people in an unprecedented manner.

It is no longer a stiff exhibit in a museum display window, nor an imagined fiction in film and television dramas, but a vivid presence that young people actively wear onto the subway, onto campuses, and into cafes.

Whenever a traditional festival comes, city parks and ancient town streets fill up with young people in ruqun and horse-face skirts, who carefully arrange their hair buns and stand holding fans, just to leave an Eastern silhouette of their own in front of the camera; these photos, spread continually through social platforms, quickly turn into a national-trend wave that cannot be ignored.
This revival is not simple retro imitation.
Many designers, while retaining traditional forms and patterns, incorporate modern tailoring and everyday fabrics, so that wide robes and big sleeves can also adapt to fast-paced urban life.
And at a deeper level, young people's fondness for Hanfu is in fact a conscious expression of cultural identity.
Through the sense of ritual in every stitch, they reconfirm where they come from.
In recent years, a fitness craze has swept through urban white-collar workers.
After work, more and more young people are no longer content to stay at home, but walk into the gym and use sweat to fight the fatigue brought on by sitting for long periods.
They often sign up for a membership eagerly at the start of the year, resolving to reshape their bodies, but those who truly keep going are only a minority.
To break through the plateau, quite a few people choose to hire a personal trainer.

A personal trainer can draw up a plan according to an individual's physique and goals, correct movements in time, and avoid exercise injuries, which to a great extent improves the safety of training, but the high cost also deters some people.
Nowadays, losing weight is no longer the only demand.
Many people regard fitness as a way of life, a way of rebuilding a sense of order amid high-pressure work.
They check in on social platforms, record changes in their weight and mood, and encourage each other, and also compare themselves with each other.
This visible perseverance makes dull repetition meaningful: what shapes the body is never a moment's resolve, but self-discipline day after day.
In an age of information explosion, data is everywhere: the poll results in the news, the health reports in our phones, the "satisfaction as high as 98%" advertised by merchants.
However, numbers seem objective, but are not necessarily reliable.
Data literacy, that is, the ability to understand, analyze and question data, is no longer the exclusive preserve of professionals.

People lacking statistical common sense are easily misled by one-sided averages or carefully selected samples: a "nationwide survey" that surveyed only fifty customers obviously has a conclusion that is not credible.
To avoid such traps, critical thinking is also needed, that is, asking where the data comes from, who collected it, and whether key background has been left out.
This ability to discern information is related to whether we can make rational choices.
Therefore, school education should incorporate data literacy into everyday courses, so that young people learn to converse rationally with numbers.
Every midsummer, sustained high temperatures often push a city's energy system to its limit.

When the temperature climbs to around forty degrees Celsius, residents' dependence on air conditioning suddenly intensifies, a peak in electricity use follows, and the grid load multiplies within a few hours in the afternoon.

To prevent large-scale blackouts, the relevant authorities have no choice but to start power-rationing measures and adjust the production plans of energy-intensive enterprises, while also urging the public to set air conditioners at around twenty-six degrees Celsius and to avoid using high-power appliances during peak electricity hours.
Although this trade-off leaves people with no good option, it is a necessary measure to guarantee residents' basic household electricity.

For ordinary citizens, the meaning of heat protection goes far beyond turning off the air conditioning: drinking water promptly, going out less at noon, and paying attention to the physical condition of the elderly and children are likewise the key to getting through the scorching summer.
In the final analysis, what extreme heat tests is not only the ability to supply electricity, but even more a city's adaptive wisdom and public governance capacity under climate pressure.
Last autumn, I began renovating the old apartment I had lived in for twenty years.
The old house had aging pipes and peeling wall plaster, and I had originally thought that as long as I said hello to the neighbors in advance, we could get along without trouble.
But things were far more difficult than I had imagined.

Downstairs lived a young couple who had just had a baby, the baby needed to sleep three hours during the day, and the noise from smashing walls and drilling happened to be concentrated in the morning.
At first they only came to my door to remind me tactfully, but later, seeing the construction hours extended again and again, they complained directly to the property management.
For a while I felt wronged, thinking that renovation simply could not be done without noise.
But when I saw that mother pacing back and forth in the stairwell holding her crying child, my heart still softened.
In the end we agreed to move the high-noise work to after two in the afternoon, and to finish half an hour earlier every day.
After the conflict was resolved, that neighbor even brought over a plate of dumplings she had made herself.
This made me understand that friction in city life often does not stem from ill will, but from a lack of mutual consideration and communication.

In recent years, shared bicycles have played a positive role in easing short-distance travel pressure and connecting with public transport, yet haphazard parking keeps encroaching on sidewalks, tactile paving and fire lanes, putting public space in front of a new governance problem.

Some users, for convenience, park their bikes at random after scanning the code, and even pile them up at residential compound gates, subway exits and around commercial districts, affecting the passage of the elderly, children and people with disabilities.

Although city regulators have tried to strengthen management through methods such as marking out geofences, adding parking spots, and collecting deposits and credit scores, because the scale of bike deployment is huge and the tidal flow is obvious, cleaning up after the fact alone often fails to work.

To solve this problem, it is necessary to promote the joint participation of companies, government and citizens, and to seek a balance between convenience and order, making urban governance more refined and inclusive.
Live-stream selling at a shopping festival like Double Eleven is, in essence, a carefully designed psychological contest.

Top streamers are not in a hurry to list product specifications, but first create a sense of scarcity: the stock number on the screen drops rapidly, the flash-sale link opens for only thirty seconds, and the countdown and the assistant host's loud reminders are interwoven, so viewers have no time at all to think.

The spend-and-save rules are then repeatedly broken down into formulas that are easy to calculate in one's head, such as "50 off for every 300 spent", and once the amount is reached, not buying instead feels like a loss.
More subtle is the control of time: the best-value bundles are often scheduled to be launched late at night, when people's rational judgment is at its weakest, and impulse buying naturally happens.
The persistently high return rate after the big sale just shows that the decision made at the moment of placing the order is more a product of emotion than of real need.
Faced with thousands upon thousands of rows of sales records, counting item by item is not only time-consuming and laborious but also extremely error-prone.
The pivot table in Excel provides an efficient solution to exactly this problem.

The user only needs to select the original data area, insert a pivot table, and then drag fields such as "region", "product" and "month" into the row, column and value areas respectively, and the system can finish summarizing by different dimensions within a few seconds, automatically working out the total sales of each region and each product.
If you only want to view a certain quarter or a certain category of product, you can also use the filter function to temporarily hide irrelevant information, making the key data clear at a glance.
In addition, when the original data is updated, you only need to click refresh and the results can be adjusted in sync, with no need to build them again.

For precisely this reason, many finance and sales staff regard the pivot table as an indispensable tool when making monthly reports, which both raises work efficiency and reduces human error, providing a reliable basis for management's decisions.

When describing the central tendency of a set of data, people are used to treating the mean, median, and mode as reliable answers, but their sensitivities are not the same, and once the distribution shape of the data is distorted, the conclusion may become misleading.

When a few extreme values pull the whole up or down, the mean loses its representativeness: most employees' monthly pay is only a few thousand yuan, but the huge compensation of a few executives makes the mean look quite considerable, and at this point the median is instead closer to the real situation.

The weakness of the mode is that it only reflects the one bracket with the highest frequency, and if the distribution is rather scattered, it cannot even indicate where the center of gravity of the data lies.

Skewed distributions are especially prone to creating illusions: in right-skewed wage and housing-price data, the mean is always dragged upward by the long tail, while the median still sits steadily at the position of most people.

Therefore, rather than asking which indicator is most accurate, it is better to first see clearly the shape of the data and then judge by combining the differences among the three, so as not to be misled by a single number.
The core of Bayesian thinking is this: when faced with new evidence, we should not completely overturn our original judgment, but should revise our beliefs prudently on that basis.
At first, the judgment we form based on existing experience is called the prior probability; the revised result obtained after absorbing new evidence is called the posterior probability.
The bridge between the two is conditional probability, that is, the likelihood of one event occurring given that another event has already occurred.
Medical testing is the most classic example.
Suppose the incidence of a certain disease is only 1%, the test can identify 90% of patients, and the proportion of healthy people misjudged as positive is about 9%.
If a person tests positive, how high is the probability that he really has the disease?
Many people intuitively think it is close to 90%, but in fact, by calculation, the posterior probability is only about 9%.
The reason is that the healthy population has an enormous base, so even if the misjudgment rate is very low, the number of false alarms still far exceeds the number of real patients.
From this it can be seen that Bayesian thinking reminds us: a conclusion depends both on the evidence itself and on the original base rate.
In scientific research, hypothesis testing is a common method for judging whether data can support a certain conclusion.

Researchers usually first set a null hypothesis of "no effect", for example that a new drug and a placebo have no difference in efficacy, and then calculate the probability of observing the current data or more extreme data on the premise that the null hypothesis holds, and this probability is the p-value.
If the p-value is lower than a significance level agreed in advance, with 0.05 being a common value, the result is called "significant", which means the null hypothesis can be rejected.
However, "significant" does not mean the effect is large, and even less does it mean the conclusion is necessarily correct.
The p-value can only indicate the degree of conflict between the data and the null hypothesis, but cannot tell us the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Even with strict standards, misjudgments can still occur: the null hypothesis is in fact true but is wrongly rejected; or an effect really exists but is not detected.

Therefore, when interpreting results, one must pay attention to the p-value and also take into account the sample size, the effect size and the study design, in order to avoid being misled by a single number.

Interestingly, the real fun at the card table often has nothing to do with winning or losing.

Customer service, however, on the grounds that the hang tag had been cut off and the packaging was worn, took the view that the goods had already affected resale and refused to handle the request.

Faced with a statistical report, people are often attracted by the eye-catching conclusion, yet overlook examining its credibility.
First, one should ask about the data source: does the data come from official registration, a professional survey, or scattered reposts on the internet?
Numbers whose source is unclear or cannot be verified, even if they look precise, are hard to find convincing.
Second, one should note whether the definitions are consistent.

For example, even for the same "unemployment rate," some count only registered unemployed people, while others also include people who have voluntarily given up looking for work; with different definitions, the results naturally differ greatly, and if the two are compared directly, one will inevitably reach a misleading judgment.
Third is sample size and sampling method.

Surveying only a few dozen people and then asserting that "most consumers are satisfied" is obviously taking a part for the whole; even if the sample size is large, if the subjects are concentrated in a certain age group, the conclusion is still biased.
Finally, one should also look at whether the report explains the survey method, the margin of error and the funding organization.
Only by weighing these aspects repeatedly will one not be led around by the nose by pretty numbers.
In the past, basketball coaches mainly relied on experience and intuition to formulate tactics, and a player's value often depended on how many points he scored.
However, with the widespread application of sports data, this situation has undergone a fundamental change.
Analysts use sensors and camera systems to record the position, defender distance and release timing of every shot, and then compare them with statistical models.
They found that although the shooting percentage beyond the three-point line is slightly lower, the expected points per attempt are higher than for most mid-range jump shots.

This finding prompted many teams to greatly increase the number of three-point attempts and reduce inefficient mid-range shots, and offensive tactics were therefore redesigned around spacing and fast passing.

At the same time, the criteria for evaluating players have become more diverse: besides scoring, teams also pay attention to defensive contributions, off-ball movement, and the team's net points while the player is on the court.
Of course, data is not omnipotent, and excellent coaches will still combine cold numbers with in-game judgment.

Near evening, she starts writing the weekly report, distilling the conclusions into concise text and accompanying them with intuitive charts, so that colleagues who do not understand technology can also understand at a glance.
In her view, the value of this job lies not in listing numbers but in making data speak, providing a reliable basis for decisions.

Although the collision was light, both parties still immediately turned on their hazard warning lights and placed warning triangles behind their cars to prevent a secondary accident.
After getting out, the drivers first checked whether anyone was injured, and then used their phones to photograph the positions of the vehicles, the points of impact and the road markings.
If the vehicles can move and no one is injured, both parties should move their cars as soon as possible to a place that does not obstruct traffic, to avoid causing congestion.

Afterwards, the parties involved can call the traffic police or apply for online handling through the traffic management platform, and the traffic police will determine liability based on the scene evidence and surveillance footage.
At the same time, the car owner should promptly report the case to the insurance company and submit materials such as the accident certificate, driver's license, vehicle license and photos.
After the insurer completes inspection and loss assessment, it will pay claims by proportion of liability.
The whole process may seem cumbersome, but as long as the evidence is complete and communication is calm, efficiency can be raised and disputes reduced.

If children accompany and communicate with them more in daily life, and communities regularly hold anti-fraud talks, both can fill the gaps in the elderly's information to a great extent.

True fraud prevention lies not in remedying things afterwards, but in that calm suspicion beforehand: hanging up the phone and verifying identity is enough to leave the scammers' tricks with nowhere to hide.

Cluster analysis offers an effective approach to this: based on data such as spending amount, purchase frequency and browsing preferences, it can group customers with similar characteristics into the same category.
As a typical unsupervised learning method, cluster analysis does not need labels to be set in advance, and the algorithm discovers hidden patterns from the data on its own.

Among these, the K-means algorithm is the most widely used: the analyst first determines the number of groups, the algorithm randomly selects a number of center points, then assigns each customer to the nearest center according to similarity, and adjusts repeatedly until the groups become stable.

After customer segmentation is completed, a company can formulate differentiated marketing strategies for different groups, for example pushing membership benefits to high-frequency consumers and issuing reactivation offers to dormant customers, thereby raising the conversion rate while keeping costs under control.

Every Spring Festival travel season, passenger flows on the national railways, highways and airlines surge sharply within a short time, putting enormous pressure on the transport authorities.
To make good arrangements for transport capacity in advance, scientific forecasting is indispensable.

Time series analysis is precisely a commonly used method for this: it takes historical passenger flow data recorded in chronological order as its object of study and extracts the underlying patterns from it.
Analysts usually break the data down into three parts.

The first is the trend, that is, the long-term direction of increase or decrease in passenger volume that appears with economic development and population movement; the second is seasonality, which refers to the periodic peaks that recur every year around the Spring Festival; the third is incidental factors, such as the fluctuations caused by extreme weather or temporary policy adjustments.
After these components are separated, the model can capture the rhythm of changes in passenger flow more accurately.
Of course, forecasting is not foolproof.

Once a sudden event occurs, historical patterns may fail, so analysts also need to combine real-time data to keep correcting the model, making the forecast results closer to reality, and thereby providing a reliable basis for ticket sales arrangements, the addition of train services and crowd control inside stations.

Recommendation algorithms have already been deeply embedded in our daily lives: when we open a news app or a short-video platform, the content presented on the home page often happens to fit our interests.

The more a user clicks on a certain type of topic, the more the system tends to push similar information, and over time their field of vision gradually narrows, as if trapped in an "information cocoon" woven from their own preferences, finding it hard to come into contact with different viewpoints.
This may not only aggravate cognitive bias, but will also weaken the basis of consensus in public discussion.

When evaluating a classification model, many beginners look only at accuracy, that is, the proportion of correctly predicted samples among all samples.
However, when the data is severely imbalanced, this metric is highly misleading.

Imagine a hospital using a model to screen for a rare disease, with only ten of a thousand people examined being ill; if the model judges everyone as "healthy", the accuracy is as high as ninety-nine percent, yet not a single patient is found.
To see the truth clearly, one needs to use a confusion matrix, which divides prediction results into four categories: true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives.
Among these, a false positive is a false alarm, that is, a healthy person being wrongly judged to be a patient.

Precision measures, among the people judged to be ill, the proportion who are truly ill, and so reflects how many false alarms there are; recall examines how many of all the real patients are successfully identified, and reflects the degree of missed diagnoses.
The two often trade off against each other, so one should weigh the choice in light of the specific scenario.

Data sharing is becoming more and more frequent, and how to protect personal privacy while realizing the value of data has become a difficult problem faced jointly by enterprises and research institutions.

Data desensitization is a common first line of defense, that is, masking, replacing or encrypting sensitive information such as names, ID numbers and mobile phone numbers, so that it can no longer point directly to a specific individual.
For example, before a hospital provides medical records to a university for research, it will first replace patients' names with random codes and blur dates of birth into age ranges.
However, merely deleting identifiers does not mean that everything is foolproof.
If an attacker cross-checks public data against information from other sources, re-identification may still be accomplished, exposing an individual's identity again.
Therefore, anonymization in the true sense requires that the processed data cannot be restored and that no specific individual can be inferred from it.
In practice, institutions must also comply with relevant regulations and establish strict approval and audit systems, to ensure that every instance of sharing meets compliance requirements.

Regrettably, the people who truly need help often hesitate for a long time to walk into a counseling room.

What stands in between is not the cost, but a deep-rooted prejudice: some equate emotional distress with weak will, and consider seeking professional support a "weak" label; others worry that once a record is left, it will draw sidelong glances and gossip from others.
So they would rather digest feelings that are hard to put into words alone, or confide in only a few relatives and friends, and thus miss the window for scientific intervention.

Facing chronic illness, people often hesitate between traditional Chinese medicine and Western medicine.

Western medicine emphasizes examination indicators, a clear cause of disease and rapid control of symptoms, and suits acute attacks or situations requiring surgery; traditional Chinese medicine, on the other hand, stresses overall regulation, helping the body restore balance through herbal medicine, acupuncture, and diet and daily routine.

When choosing, you should first look at the stage of the disease: if the condition is critical, you should seek medical care promptly, with Western medicine treatment as the main approach; if the symptoms are stable, you can combine traditional Chinese medicine regulation under a doctor's guidance.
Patients should also understand their own constitution, history of drug allergies and past treatment effects, and should not blindly trust folk remedies.
Recovery from chronic illness is often long, and requires regular follow-up checks, a regular routine and patient perseverance.
Whichever approach you choose, you should take safety, effectiveness and sustainability as principles, so that treatment truly serves the improvement of quality of life.
In business reports and news coverage, misleading charts are a common sight, and the most common technique among them is truncating the vertical axis.
Suppose a company announces its sales for two years: last year was 980000 yuan and this year is 1020000 yuan, an actual increase of only about 4%.

However, if the chart maker does not let the vertical axis start from zero but starts marking from 970000 yuan, the heights of the two bars will differ greatly, this year's bar will look about five times last year's, and a tiny fluctuation is thereby exaggerated into a startling leap.

The root of the problem is that a bar chart relies on the length of the bars to convey quantity, and length should be proportional to value; once the vertical axis is truncated, the visual proportion and the true proportion are completely disconnected, and the reader's intuition is misled along with it.

To avoid being fooled, we should develop the habit of first looking at the starting point and scale of the vertical axis, and then checking against the specific numbers to judge whether the difference is really that large.
Improving the ability to read charts is not only a basic skill of statistics, but also an essential quality of rational judgment in the information age.
The core of data visualization lies not in whether a chart is attractive, but in whether it lets readers quickly grasp the essence of the information.
Before choosing a chart, you should first be clear about what you want to express.

If you want to compare the differences between categories, such as the quarterly sales of each department, a bar chart is the most intuitive, because the human eye is especially sensitive to differences in the height of bars.

If you want to present the trend of data changing over time, such as a city's temperature fluctuations over a year, a line chart is more suitable, and a continuous line can clearly show the direction of rises and falls.

As for the pie chart, it is suited to showing the proportion each part makes up of the whole, but once there are more than five or six categories, the slices will look crowded and readers will find it hard to tell them apart.
In addition, whichever chart you use, you must clearly label the names and units of the axes, and avoid truncating the axis to exaggerate differences, otherwise it easily misleads the audience.
In the job-seeking process, an interview is not only a chance to show one's abilities, but also an important step in judging whether a position suits oneself.

When preparing for an interview, a job seeker should first research the company's background, the job responsibilities, and industry development, and then, combining them with their own experience, put together clear project cases.
In addition, job seekers can learn the salary range for similar positions through recruitment platforms and industry reports, and thereby state more reliable expectations.
Faced with the salary question, many people easily become nervous, but in fact, after understanding market conditions, they can use data to show their own value.
When negotiating, besides monthly pay, also watch the five insurances and one fund, probation length, performance bonuses, and overtime arrangements.

If the current job lacks room for growth, changing jobs may be a reasonable choice, but the premise is to assess the risks fully and to clarify each benefit with the new employer, so as to avoid misunderstandings after starting work.
The small matter of lunch can often best reflect a person's way of life.

Every day at noon, two completely different choices always appear in the office: one group of people pour into the company canteen, seeking convenience and liveliness; the other group insist on bringing their own meals, using the time left over from the night before to buy themselves some calm.
Looking at cost-effectiveness alone, the canteen seems to have the advantage: no shopping, no cooking, a meal settled by swiping a card, with the time cost compressed to the minimum.
However, people who rely on the canteen for a long time often complain that the flavours are monotonous and the food too oily and salty, and health risks accumulate without their noticing.

By contrast, the packed-lunch crowd can independently control the source and proportions of their ingredients, with little oil and salt and a balance of meat and vegetables, which both looks after the stomach and saves a considerable amount of expense each month.
Of course, bringing food is not without cost; the toil of getting up early to prepare a meal and the queuing in front of the microwave are both realities that must be accepted.

True wisdom perhaps lies not in taking sides, but in flexible allocation: mainly the canteen on workdays, and a packed lunch for variety when tired, letting saving money and health reach reconciliation at the same table.
In the early stage of an epidemic, one of the indicators public health departments care about most is the reproduction number, that is, the average number of people one infected person can infect.
When this value is greater than one, cases will grow exponentially; once it falls below one, the epidemic can be expected to ease gradually.

To anticipate the trend, researchers use modeling, bring variables such as population movement, incubation period and prevention and control measures into the calculation, and simulate the development trajectories under different scenarios.
However, a model's reliability depends on the quality of the data: if testing coverage is insufficient or reporting is delayed, the results may deviate from reality.
The so-called inflection point refers to the turning moment when new cases change from rising continuously to falling continuously.
Its appearance often means that the prevention and control measures are beginning to show results, but it does not mean the risk has been eliminated.
If controls are relaxed too early, the reproduction number may rebound again, causing the earlier efforts to be wasted at the last step.
Decision-makers must not only interpret the curve, but also weigh carefully between scientific judgment and social cost.
Open your phone, and that face in the front camera, retouched by a beauty algorithm, is quietly reshaping many people's perception of their own appearance.

Filters smooth skin until it has no texture and sharpen the jawline, and over time people begin to treat this virtual perfection as the standard, while their real selves instead become flaws that need repairing.
This gap has given rise to appearance anxiety: some people repeatedly compare the proportions of their features, and some lose sleep all night over a single photo.

Under anxiety, medical aesthetics has gone from the choice of a few to a topic for the masses, and minor-adjustment, light-and-laser, and injection procedures are packaged as "shortcuts to becoming beautiful" and are constantly displayed and imitated on social platforms.
What deserves vigilance is that when appearance is simplified into a set of quantifiable indicators, a person's worth is compressed along with it.

True confidence does not come from endlessly approaching the filter, but stems from accepting one's own uniqueness: acknowledging that one has imperfections, yet still being willing to face the camera calmly.
Hosting a family banquet at my in-laws' home for the first time, I was especially cautious.

My mother-in-law said that although the seating order at a round table is unwritten, it has its own sense of proportion: my father-in-law sits in the main seat directly facing the door, my mother-in-law is on his left, so she can look after the guests; my husband and I sit near the kitchen, convenient for adding soup and serving dishes.

Before the meal begins, if the elders do not pick up their chopsticks, the younger ones cannot eat first; if a guest arrives late, one should also first explain to the elders, and then greet the guest quietly, to avoid an awkward scene.

When toasting, I first raise my glass with both hands, with the rim slightly lower than the rim of the elders' glasses, and then say a few polite words, thanking them for looking after me in daily life.
My husband reminded me that when toasting my mother-in-law, I must not only urge her to drink, but also drink some on her behalf, so she is not put in a difficult position.
These rules seem tedious, but in fact they all express respect and consideration.
Only when I act accordingly do I feel at ease.
In recent years, the marathon has gradually gone from a niche sport into urban life, becoming a way for many ordinary people to challenge themselves and make friends.

Every race season, the registration system often has its slots become scarce soon after opening, and people not only care about results but also look forward to feeling the rhythm of the city while running.
Many amateur runners join running clubs, train together on weekends, and learn how to control their pace, avoiding burning up their energy too fast right from the start.
For them, finishing a race is not only for getting a medal, but even more a confirmation of self-discipline and perseverance.
In a running club there are both experienced pace leaders and newcomers who have just started, and everyone reminds one another about refueling, warming up and recovery.
In the park in the early morning, runners record their mileage and heart rate, share training plans, and also learn to be with themselves during long-distance running.
Behind the marathon craze is reflected city people's search for a healthy life, emotional regulation and a sense of community belonging.
In recent years, online consultations and home delivery of medicine have gradually blended into people's daily lives.

For patients with chronic illness, the long process of going back and forth to the hospital, queuing to register and waiting to be seen and collect medicine is itself a drain; now you only need to open your phone, choose a compliant internet hospital, talk with a doctor by video and upload examination reports, and you can obtain a diagnostic opinion in a short time.

After the doctor issues an electronic prescription, the medicine is delivered to your home by a partner pharmacy, and part of the cost can also be settled online through medical insurance, so the patient's financial burden is reduced accordingly.

The rise of this model reflects the deep-seated contradiction of the uneven distribution of medical resources: high-quality doctors are concentrated in big cities, while residents of remote areas often have nowhere to turn for treatment.
Technology has not eliminated this gap, but has provided a path across it.

Of course, online consultation has its limits after all: it is good at handling common illnesses, follow-up prescriptions and health management, but cannot replace face-to-face palpation and emergency treatment.
Looking rationally at its convenience and its limitations may be the most fitting attitude in the age of digital healthcare.

In the city center, many old residential compounds were built in the 1980s and 1990s, and at the planning stage almost no one anticipated that private cars would become so widespread, so the ratio of parking spaces is seriously insufficient.

Today, difficulty parking has become one of the thorniest conflicts in residents' daily lives: in the evening, both sides of the narrow passageways are packed with vehicles, and even the fire lanes are gradually eaten away by vehicles parked in them, so that if an accident suddenly occurs, rescue vehicles can hardly pass.

Owners accuse the property management of inaction, while the property management claims it has no law enforcement power itself, the two sides each stick to their own story, and the dispute continues year after year.

Some communities have tried staggered-time sharing of parking spaces at nearby shopping malls, or introduced license plate recognition systems to regulate entry and exit, with fairly good results; however, the more fundamental predicament is that the redistribution of public space inevitably touches each household's interests, and how to strike a balance between fairness and efficiency still depends on long negotiation and compromise.

Today's young people have fallen into an intriguing contradiction: their daytime hours are filled with work and entertainment, and only the late night truly belongs to them, so staying up late has become a habit they cannot give up; yet the fatigue and weariness that appear when they look in the mirror in the morning give them an almost devout enthusiasm for health preservation.
Goji berries steep in thermos cups and all kinds of health supplements sit on office desks; these almost ritualized acts seem enough to offset the overdraft of the night before.

But this way of life, squandering health on one hand and desperately trying to make up for it on the other, precisely reflects the widespread anxiety of sub-health: the body has not yet shown a clear illness, but keeps sending signals of fatigue, insomnia and scattered attention.
True health preservation perhaps does not depend on how many goji berries you have, but on whether you are willing to admit that health is never a debt that can be redeemed afterwards.
For many Beijing drifters, sharing a flat is almost an unavoidable choice when first arriving in this city.
The expense of renting alone often takes up most of one's income, while sharing a flat can press living costs down to a bearable range.

An old apartment originally designed for a family of three is partitioned by the landlord with plasterboard into four or five partition rooms of under ten square metres, each of which holds only a bed and a desk.
What sharing a flat brings is not only savings.

When the living room, kitchen and bathroom are shared by four or five people, personal privacy gives way to mutual accommodation: who uses the bathroom first, who should take out the rubbish, how loud the footsteps of someone coming home late at night are, have all become topics that need repeated negotiation.
Many flatmates go from being complete strangers to gradually becoming familiar, will share food from their hometowns, and will also leave a light on when the other works overtime.
There are also people who always maintain a polite distance, and after living together for a year cannot say clearly what the other's job is.
This aloofness is not necessarily indifference, and is more like a kind of self-protection -- after all, the next rent increase may force one to move out at any time.

In the course of enterprise digital transformation, data is often scattered across the order system, the customer management system and various log files, in inconsistent formats and of uneven quality.
To make this data truly serve decision-making, it is necessary to integrate it with the help of the ETL process.
ETL is an abbreviation formed from the initial letters of the three English words extract, transform and load.
First comes extraction, that is, reading the required data from each source system according to established rules, while trying to avoid interfering with the normal operation of business systems.

Second comes transformation, in which data engineers clean and deduplicate the raw data, unify the formats of dates and currencies, and calculate new indicators according to business logic, so as to eliminate contradictions and redundancy.
Last comes loading, in which the processed data is written into the data warehouse for analysts to query and generate reports.
These three stages are interlocking and together form an automatically running data pipeline.

The pipeline can be executed on a schedule, hourly or daily, and once an error occurs in any stage, the system will issue an alert, reminding technical staff to investigate promptly, thereby ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the data.
Algorithmic bias is often mistaken for a flaw in the technology itself, but in fact it often originates from social prejudices hidden in the training data.

Take the recruitment screening system developed by a multinational company as an example: engineers trained the model with hiring records from the past ten years, and men account for the vast majority of these records.
As a result, the system gradually linked "male" with "excellent candidate" and automatically lowered the scores of résumés containing female-related experience.
This seemingly objective judgment has in fact entrenched and amplified historical discrimination.

What is more troublesome is that most algorithms are like a "black box", and users find it hard to know the basis of their decisions; the lack of transparency lets the problem go unnoticed for a long time.

To improve fairness, on the one hand it is necessary to take into account the representativeness of different groups when collecting training data, and on the other hand an independent review mechanism should be established, with evaluation standards made public, so that those affected have the right to question and appeal.
The university dormitory is where many young people experience collective living for the first time.
Roommates from different regions and with different habits are assigned under the same roof, living together day and night.
However, it is precisely this close contact that often plants the seeds of conflict without anyone noticing.
Differences in daily schedules are especially prominent: some people are used to studying late into the night by lamplight, while others get up and get busy at dawn.
When one person needs quiet to fall asleep while the other is still tapping on a keyboard, friction quietly arises.
In addition, trivial matters such as uneven division of cleaning and casually borrowing belongings may also become the fuse of accumulated resentment.
It is worth noting that these conflicts are not irreconcilable.
What truly determines the atmosphere of a dormitory is whether roommates are willing to be considerate of each other and communicate frankly.

If everyone stubbornly holds to their own boundaries and refuses to put themselves in others' shoes, even the smallest disagreement will turn into an impassable chasm; conversely, as long as everyone is willing to set common rules and respect each other's pace of life, collective living can move from adjustment to harmony.
Before any data analysis work begins, data cleaning is a checkpoint that cannot be bypassed.
Raw data often comes from multiple channels in inconsistent formats, with a large number of missing values mixed in: some fields were omitted, or the recorder simply left them blank.
If these gaps are directly treated as zero, the conclusions will be distorted, so the analyst must decide: whether to discard the entire record, or to infer a reasonable value from the context.
Duplicate values are equally thorny.

The same customer is registered several times in different systems, which looks like a sufficient sample but in fact exaggerates the weight of certain groups and skews the statistical results toward a false prosperity.
Outliers test judgment even more: it may be an entry error, or it may be an extreme phenomenon truly worth tracking, and hasty deletion amounts to erasing the most valuable clue.
From this it can be seen that preprocessing is not a mechanical technical operation, but a deliberation about trade-offs.
If the cleaning is too aggressive, the data loses its original texture; if too lenient, noise will drown the signal.
A truly mature practitioner can always find that subtle line between the two.
For many young people, obtaining a driver's license is almost regarded as a necessary rite of passage into adulthood.
However, only after actually entering driving school do people discover that this process is far longer than imagined.

In theory, as long as one passes the written tests of Subject One and Subject Four and then completes the actual road driving of Subject Three, that is enough to get a license; but in fact, a large number of candidates stop at Subject Two.

Items such as reverse parking into a garage, parallel parking and hill starts seem to be merely mechanical operations, yet they require candidates to judge precisely, in a cramped space, the distance between the body of the car and the boundary lines.

Instructors repeatedly stress the importance of "reference points", but once the test-site environment differs slightly from the practice ground, nervous candidates easily become flustered, and may even lose all their earlier effort because of a single line touch.

It is precisely for this reason that quite a few people regard the driving test as a dual test of patience and mindset: it measures not only driving skill, but even more whether a person can stay calm under pressure.
Every Spring Festival travel rush, railway passenger volume surges, and many migrant workers, students and people visiting relatives all hope to return home as soon as possible.
Especially around the Spring Festival, the station waiting halls are always packed with people dragging luggage, and the mood of heading home is particularly urgent.
Because tickets on popular routes are in short supply, grabbing tickets becomes a race against time.
People usually open 12306 in advance, refresh the train listings repeatedly, and compare the times, prices and remaining tickets of high-speed and ordinary trains.
Once tickets go on sale, many people click to buy at the same time, hoping to grab the most suitable train.
If they fail to get a ticket right away, passengers can also submit a waitlist order and wait for the system to automatically match returned tickets or newly added seats.
For most people, the Spring Festival travel rush is not only a journey but also an arrangement connected with family reunion, so what lies behind grabbing tickets is anticipation of home.
During the Second World War, the military wanted to add armor to bombers, but could not cover the whole aircraft, or the fuselage would be too heavy and the plane could not fly far.

Engineers counted the bullet holes on returning aircraft and found that the holes were densest on the wings and tail, while there were very few near the engines and cockpit, so some people advocated reinforcing the parts with many bullet holes.

However, a statistician put forward the opposite view: this data came only from aircraft that had successfully returned, while aircraft that were hit in a vital spot and could not fly back had not entered the statistics at all.
In other words, the reason there are few bullet holes near the engines is not that those spots are hard to hit, but that most aircraft hit there crashed.
This phenomenon of reaching one-sided conclusions because of improper sample selection is called survivorship bias.
It is a common logical fallacy, which makes us, when attributing causes, look only at the visible successful ones while ignoring the silent failures.
In the fiercely competitive retail industry, shelves are by no means arranged casually, but are the result of repeated deliberation over data.
Supermarkets collect customers' checkout records and, through basket analysis, find out which products are often bought together.
Its core is association rules, that is, extracting from a large number of transactions the pattern that "people who bought A often also buy B."

The most famous case is "beer and diapers": it is said that young fathers, after getting off work, buy diapers for their children and often take some beer along while they are at it, so merchants displayed the two closer together, and sales rose accordingly.
Whether this story is true is still disputed, but it vividly illustrates the value of data.

Nowadays, merchants adjust their displays based on similar analyses: they put milk at the very back of the store, making customers walk through the whole aisle; they place bread and jam next to each other, stimulating additional purchases.
